highlights.title: Pocket's AI made my game ideas real. Now Meta controls the results.
highlights.summary: The relatively recent rise of AI-assisted coding tools and the whole concept of "vibe coding" have effectively upended entire software development workflows. While these tools have been available to novice coders willing to put in the work to set them up, those with little to no coding experience…
body: Meta's latest AI-based project launch wants to make that kind of vibe coding as instantly accessible as posting on social media. Pocket—which launched in the US last Friday, August 21, after Meta acquired the staff behind the now-defunct vibe-coding app Gizmo in March—is a mobile app that lets users create fully functional interactive "gizmos" just by typing prompts into a text box, without even the option to look at a line of code. Those gizmos can then be shared with the world in a TikTok-style endless scroll complete with likes, comments, reposts, and all the other hallmarks of social media addiction.

After playing around with Pocket for the better part of a week, I found myself getting hooked on the simple process of quickly standing up functional, relatively feature-rich game prototypes simply by chatting with an LLM. But the result of all that time and AI effort is a couple of interactive toys that are effectively trapped in Meta's new walled garden, without any real way to turn them into something separate.

highlights.title: How an MIT research project became a global programming language
highlights.summary: With millions of users across the world, Julia has been used to conduct cutting-edge research and to design new drugs, jet engines, heat pumps, and more.

It all started with some exasperated emails. Back in 2009, a group of researchers began venting their frustration with the programming languages designed to help scientists and other researchers perform complex mathematical operations and statistical simulations without learning how to code. These programming languages were rigid and slow. If scientists built something that really worked, they’d need to rewrite the entire program in another language just to run it more quickly.

The emails turned into a research project at MIT with the mission of building an easy-to-use, high-performance programming language called Julia, which is designed for scientific research, data analysis, and modeling complex systems such as jet engines, drugs, financial markets, and robots, to name a few examples.

highlights.title: Halloween: The Game Gets Denied a Rating in Yet Another Country
highlights.summary: It's not only fans in Australia who will have to sit on the sidelines and watch others play Halloween: The Game when it launches on Sept. 9. In Japan, Halloween: The Game won't be available on PlayStation, as it has been denied a rating from the Computer Entertainment Rating Organization (CERO)…
body: For a game to launch in Japan, it needs a domestic rating from CERO. If CERO refuses to rate a game, companies will have to work around this and instead try to obtain a rating from the International Age Rating Coalition (IARC), which makes it possible for games to be sold digitally when CERO denies a rating. However, even that option won't make Halloween: The Game available for PS5 users in Japan.

Thanks to its IARC rating, Halloween: The Game will be available on Xbox and PC. Regarding the PlayStation release, in March 2022, Sony changed its policies so the PS Store in Japan would accept IARC-rated games. However, CERO ratings were still required for physical releases or for digital releases rated 18+. Since Halloween has been deemed a mature game in Japan due to its "visceral violence and nudity," it requires a CERO rating in order to launch on the PS Store.

highlights.title: Parasomnia review – sleep-schedule horror conjures up a succubus on the loose in waking nightmare
highlights.summary: Debut director James Ross II shows promise in this gore fest, but the fear factor suffers from an overly complex plot. Sleep has been part of the horror genre repertoire since The Cabinet of Dr Caligari, and the anxieties around it are spiking as the “ sleep economy ” becomes a thing.
body: The levels of cause and effect, reality and fantasy, in Riley’s dreams are confusing at first: she inhabits the perspective of the eyeball-plucking fiend (a nod to ETA Hoffmann’s Sandman?) and wanders a hellish labyrinth in which past victims are trapped. Thankfully, Ross clarifies everything with a burst of guiding lore in an ingenious third-act switchback that revises the previous two acts.

Despite this sturdy constriction, the film remains only mildly scary – maybe because of the interruptions and vagaries of the complex setup. The middling performances don’t feel extreme enough, and the generic, chalk-faced, taloned bogeyman is a mere stain on Freddy Krueger’s jersey. But there is an undeniable astuteness and agility in the storytelling here on which Ross can build.
points: Debut director James Ross II shows promise in this gore fest, but the fear factor suffers from an overly complex plot.

highlights.title: ATM Flaws Reveal Key Weaknesses in the Software Supply Chain
highlights.summary: A security researcher discovered nine vulnerabilities impacting ATM encryption and authentication software. But the problems extend far beyond your local cash machine.
body: For the past five years, security researcher Matt Burch has immersed himself in the esoteric and high-stakes world of ATM security, in which small software flaws can sometimes expose cold, hard cash. As Burch has bored deeper into the computers powering these digital lock boxes—and continued to find vulnerabilities in key digital security systems—he has started working to raise the alarm, not just about overlooked ATM flaws, but about how that same software used in other industries can introduce weaknesses in an array of critical systems.

At the Black Hat and Defcon security conferences in Las Vegas this month, Burch presented findings about nine vulnerabilities that have been fixed in disk encryption and pre-boot authentication software called CryptoPro Secure Disk. The flaws could have been exploited to bypass CryptoPro's integrity checks and gain full access to encrypted devices.

highlights.summary: A white paper gives research groups four priority models, each of which uses artificial intelligence differently.

As artificial intelligence pervades scientific research, journals, institutions and classrooms are all adopting their own rules on how to use large language models. But how can individual laboratories decide on the best ways to use AI to enhance their work? It depends on the research values that your team prioritizes, a white paper suggests.

The paper, posted on the arXiv preprint server by a team of space-science researchers in July 1 and not yet peer reviewed, suggests that there’s no one-size-fits-all strategy for adopting AI policies across research groups. Instead, the authors define four lab-group ‘archetypes’, each of which could benefit from using AI during different phases of the research process.

The movie will be animated by CloverWorks ( Spy x Family, The Elusive Samurai ), directed by Katsuhiko Kitada ( Evangelion: 2.0 You Can (Not) Advance ), with character design by Akemi Hayashi ( Banana Fish ).

Pokémon: Wild Card will be the 25th movie in the franchise (including 2019's live-action Detective Pikachu ), and the first to follow 2020's Pokémon the Movie: Secrets of the Jungle. highlights.title: The pet I’ll never forget: Jerry, the king of dogs, who taught me how to live
highlights.summary: After a burglary, my parents decided we needed extra security. Jerry was the answer – and this hungry, handsome hound helped us all in countless ways. Jerry came into our lives because a burglar had broken in. My mum had woken in the middle of the night to find an intruder in our kitchen.
body: Jerry was very laid-back and Zen. He became part of the family straight away. He also became the therapy dog we hadn’t realised we needed. With two teenagers in the house (me and my older brother) and a hyperactive younger brother, someone was always in a strop and needing to let off steam by taking him out for a walk. Each time, Jerry obliged. I’d bore him with my latest teen-romance trauma; he was a very good listener. Sometimes, he’d have five walks a day, with both of my parents taking their turn. He certainly got his steps in.

He also dined in style. Most dogs loiter under the table during meal times. Jerry would climb on top of it and make himself comfortable until dinner was served. Often, I would come home from school and catch him lying there regally, waiting for his next banquet. It wasn’t scraps that interested him; he wanted the full three courses. He particularly liked deli food – salt beef, potato salad, pastrami, coleslaw, even apple strudel. One day, a big bowl of chopped liver disappeared. My mum blamed me, my brothers, then my dad, before realising who the culprit was.

highlights.title: The U.S. is building barriers around drones and robots, but China has scale to get around them
highlights.summary: The U.S. is shutting out more foreign-made drones and robots. China’s scale means the global competition may simply move elsewhere.
body: In July and August, Washington tightened restrictions on foreign-made advanced robotic systems and imposed steep tariffs on imported drones and their components, both moves citing national-security concerns. The drone tariffs take effect in September, with additional component tariffs following in 2027.

These moves are part of a broader U.S. effort to restrict foreign technology in strategically important industries. The FCC’s Covered List, established in 2021, initially targeted telecommunications and surveillance equipment from companies including Huawei, ZTE and Hikvision before expanding to foreign-made drones and, most recently, to advanced robotic devices.
The latest move comes as Chinese manufacturers have built commanding positions in both drones and humanoid robots, often competing at prices U.S. and European rivals struggle to match.

Taken together, the restrictions are raising a bigger question for the global robotics industry: If Chinese drones and humanoids are increasingly shut out of the U.S., where does the competition move next?

highlights.title: Do you have a bespoke ‘dirty zone’? | Emma Beddington
highlights.summary: Apparently a dedicated mud room will make you less stressed. But I have a very different approach. I was excited to learn that the latest interiors essential, according to the Washington Post, is a “dirty zone”.
body: Does this make me kinda chic? Unfortunately not: the Post is actually preaching the benefits of confining the sordid ephemera of life to carefully delineated and hidden areas: storage benches, monogrammed totes or even a “mud room” (for coats, shoes, skis, lacrosse sticks and dog-washing sinks – I think posh Britons call it a boot room). A 2021 study in the Netherlands found that participants who did chores in chaotic environments had higher levels of the stress marker salivary alpha-amylase. I always wonder what’s brewing in my mouth as I fall over piles of filthy shoes yet again while running to answer the door.

This dirty zone system sounds nice, but deeply, decadently unrealistic. A mud room, rather than various rooms containing some mud, surely isn’t something most people have. If you do, apparently you’ll also want a $115 (£85) petitgrain and neroli reed diffuser, to help mask the smell. One expert consulted by the Post suggested green as a mud room colour scheme, to coordinate harmoniously with your brown delivery boxes “if you’re a heavy Amazon shopper”, which has a real last-days-of-Rome ring to it.

highlights.title: Texas Governor Abbott blocks funding for more Flock cameras
highlights.summary: As backlash grows over Flock's AI surveillance cameras, Texas Governor Greg Abbott has frozen state spending on them. The move came just ahead of the publication of a Texas Tribune investigation that revealed the state spent over $30 million on Flock cameras.
body: Flock cameras have increasingly drawn ire from across the political spectrum as they’ve become the subject of privacy concerns. There have been multiple incidents of officers being placed on leave or criminally charged for misusing Flock systems, including at least six in Texas alone. The company has also come under scrutiny for its data-sharing, the placement of some of its cameras near playgrounds, its own employees’ access to video feeds, unsecured video feeds, and its ham-fisted attempts to avoid transparency.

In recent months, cities around the country have been canceling their contracts with Flock, including many in Texas. Abbott’s Democratic opponent in the race for governor, Gina Hinojosa, has criticized him for expanding use of the cameras in the state. And Republican representative Keith Self recently posted on Instagram that, “From Flock cameras to kill switches, we will NOT surrender our Fourth Amendment rights to the growing surveillance state.” Cheering on the destruction of Flock cameras has even become a unifying pastime on the internet.

highlights.title: AI could cause global economic downturn, Bank of England governor tells G20
highlights.summary: Andrew Bailey, in role as financial stability watchdog chief, warns advanced models risk destabilising system. The Bank of England’s governor, Andrew Bailey, has joined the throng of figures warning about the global risks posed by the most advanced artificial intelligence technology.
body: In a two-page letter sent to international finance ministers and central bank governors as part of his role as chair of the international Financial Stability Board (FSB), Bailey said “frontier” AI models were “showing increasingly sophisticated autonomy and problem-solving abilities, as well as threat capabilities”.
He said the models risked destabilising the “highly interconnected” global financial system via cyber-disruption that “can spread across jurisdictions”.

Bailey wrote to G20 finance ministers and central bank governors before their meeting in North Carolina, US, this week: “Recent developments have also highlighted to me that many jurisdictions do not have the protocols in place to manage the development, release, and deployment of advanced frontier AI models, heightening risks for the financial sector and beyond”.

His letter adds to alarm bells about AI that have been sounded by prominent technologists over the past few weeks – and mirrors his previous calls for international cooperation to tackle growing AI threats, when he told City bosses: “No country can seal itself off from the cross-border nature of systems that are prevalent today.”

highlights.title: Doctors’ AI scribes get names of drugs and diagnoses wrong, NHS watchdog warns
highlights.summary: Exclusive: Patients identify errors in consultation transcripts that are missed by GPs, Healthwatch England finds. AI technology that listens to and transcribes patients’ consultations with doctors can put them at risk by getting the names of drugs and illnesses wrong, an NHS watchdog has warned.
body: In one case a woman was left badly shaken when the AI scribe’s summary of her conversation wrongly said she had demyelination – serious nerve damage that can lead to multiple sclerosis.
It was only when the patient, an NHS health professional, queried the AI tool’s record of the result of her MRI scan that the hospital corrected it to what it should have been – “null demyelination”.
“This was eventually corrected but was a very traumatising experience to be given an incorrect diagnosis because of AI and then be told it’s a typo,” said the woman, who asked not to be named.

Healthwatch England has highlighted the case and other mistakes by AI scribes to show that the technology, which the NHS is rolling out rapidly, is a potential threat to patient safety. Unless detected, errors could end up in patients’ medical records and affect their care, it said.

highlights.title: Musk’s faster path to more gas turbines comes with pollution problem
highlights.summary: Elon Musk says a secretive new SpaceX foundry will let him cast his own turbine blades and get gas power online 18 months faster than anyone else — but it's a bet on a fuel source that's already triggering lawsuits and health studies everywhere his (and others') turbines have gone in.
body: Elon Musk says he’s found a way to solve one of AI’s biggest bottlenecks by making a hard-to-manufacture turbine part himself.

“SpaceX and Tesla are each building 100GW/year of solar production capacity as fast as possible,” Musk wrote on X on Saturday, “but natural gas will still be needed to supplement and bootstrap solar for several years. The limiting factor for nat gas turbine production is casting the blades & vanes. By doing in-house casting at SpaceX, we can accelerate nat gas turbines coming online by up to 18 months, which is a profound game-changer.”

The “why” of all this goes back to one of the biggest challenges facing the AI industry right now. GPU shortages are still an issue — Nvidia’s newest Blackwell chips are still running lead times of several months, for example — but a second constraint has emerged alongside it, which is the physical power grid. The International Energy Agency projects global data center electricity use will roughly double by 2030, and gas turbine maker GE Vernova says it’s essentially sold out of production capacity through 2030 due largely to AI infrastructure demand.

highlights.title: 12TB of Steam Files Leak as a Decade’s Worth of First- and Third-Party Game Data Is Exposed
highlights.summary: Approximately 12TB of data has been reportedly extracted from Steam, which apparently encompasses everything that was published on the platform between 2003 and 2013. According to Valve-related content creator Gabe Follower, the data has allegedly been gathered via a publicly accessible endpoint…
body: Gabe Follower notes this data includes the entire Steam library from the period between 2003 and 2013 – not just Valve games. The 12TB of data is said to contain both complete games and beta versions of games, and a variety of early and unseen prototype versions of games that were placed on Steam sometime within that 10-year period have already been uncovered by archivists, enthusiasts, and other interested parties. For instance, those digging have found a build of Left 4 Dead from several months prior to its actual release which features a different HUD, voice lines which never featured in the retail version, and sections of the map that were subsequently altered.
With the sheer size of the leaked data pile, it’s likely more such information will be revealed as people search through it.

highlights.title: Why the Hottest New Wearables Want to Be Ignored
highlights.summary: Burnt out on wrist buzzes and notification overload? A new crop of minimalist wearables promises to collect your health data without demanding your attention.
body: There’s a new kind of gadget on shelves, designed for you to ignore it 99 percent of the time—it only needs attention when its battery is low. I'm talking about the screen-free wearable. You rarely look at it or touch it, yet it collects health stats day and night so you can view them later on in an app, when you get the time—if you can find the time. No pressure.

They have been exploding of late and are only set to grab more attention in the coming months, with the promise of demanding less of your attention once you actually buy one. Today there’s the Garmin Cirqa, Google Fitbit Air, Polar Loop, the Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Whoop series, the original pioneer of this category. Apple is considering its own version of the concept, according to Bloomberg. One answer to that big question of why? Many of us are sick of attention-hoarding tech and social media, not least realizing it is probably doing us no good.

highlights.title: 1666: Amsterdam's developer says it 'won't be using AI anymore', and the tech was only used 'in conception and pre-production'—arguably the most creative phase of the entire process
highlights.summary: There was surprise and delight when Summer Game Fest brought the reveal of 1666: Amsterdam, the long awaited dream project from Assassin's Creed co-creator Patrice Désilets.
body: Désilets' studio Panache Digital Games copped to using AI in the production of certain assets, then apologised and promised to remove those elements in time for the early access launch. With that launch happening last week, Désilets now says that Panache has decoupled AI from its pipeline entirely and it won't be using AI in future.

Speaking to GamesRadar+, Désilets stressed that Panache was done with generative AI, and claimed that most of the AI used occurred in the early stages of the project. "Yes, we use some AI in the process, mostly at the beginning," Désilets explained. "In conception and pre-production. It's been totally removed and we won't be using it anymore."

As someone who likes their art made by, y'know, artists, I'm glad that Panache has done what it can to scrape generative AI out of 1666: Amsterdam. That said, it irks me when developers say they only used AI at the concepting stage of development, because that's the most fun and rewarding part of any creative project.

highlights.title: ‘Sometimes you just need a good cry’: why Little Women is my feelgood movie
highlights.summary: The latest in our series of writers highlighting their go-to comfort films is an ode to the teary 1994 adaptation of the classic novel. I have an ongoing argument with some friends about how I refuse to watch Interstellar again, despite considering it a beautiful and well-crafted film.
body: But at the same time, the movie I choose as my feelgood film is one that has reduced me to a sobbing, snotty mess time and time again, whether I’m watching it curled up with my cat on the couch, swaddled in blankets while sick in bed or jostling with my seatmate for the armrest on an airplane. And just like with the score from Interstellar, the moment I hear Thomas Newman’s wistful little oboe intro of the 1994 version of Little Women, I can feel my eyes well up with tears.

As you’ve probably discerned already, I tend to feel things very strongly. Probably one of my most psychotic traits is that I have to spoil the endings of most movies before I watch them for the first time because if I get too attached to a character and that character dies, it could take me several days to recover. But sometimes you just need a good cry, and that’s exactly what Gillian Armstrong’s Little Women is for me.
